newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spain economic growth weak but seen improving.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain economic growth weak but seen improving.

text.p: A rise in unemployment and Bank of Spain forecasts of unchanged third quarter growth on Friday appeared to reveal an economy growing less vibrantly than top officials have recently suggested.
But many economists believe the Bank of Spain is right on track when it forecasts improvement in coming months.
On Friday, Spain announced that unemployment had risen in October to 14.08 percent from 13.82 percent in September, although the number of new job placements hit a record monthly high of 912,972.
Separately, the Bank of Spain forecast that third-quarter domestic product had grown about two percent, little changed from 1.9 percent in the second quarter.

"With the available data for this period, we estimate that year-on-year quarterly growth of real gross domestic product will have been of the order of two percent, not very different from the past two quarters either in magnitude or in composition," the Bank of Spain said in its monthly report.
Domestic demand could also have risen by two percent, slightly above 1.8 percent in the previous quarter. Private consumption was seen stagnant compared to the first half.
Economists said the news and forecasts appeared more sombre than might have been suggested by the tone of Bank of Spain Governor Luis Angel Rojo or Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato just one day ago.

"They are telling us the economy is picking up, but it's a forecast. There is very little to base it on. It's wishful thinking," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid. "The economy is weak."
"The economic situation is fairly favourable," Rojo told a seminar on Thursday.
Rato said the economy had entered a recovery phase in the third quarter, and added that the improved domestic economic situation had been aided by a recovery in confidence and in credibility.

Both Rato and Rojo emphasised that Spain was shaping up well economically for the key single currency tests in 1997, when it must meet stringent criteria on inflation, long-term interest rates, deficit, debt and currency stability.
There are no requirements on employment.
Economist Gregorio Gomez echoed these views.

"Is the situation good when the unemployment rate doesn't go down?. Financial markets are improving but I don't see that the real economy is going in the same direction and that is what is finally going to count for convergence," Gomez said.
For Lumholdt, Rojo's comments were "suspiciously in line with the government. I smell a rate cut coming. He's talking the party line."
The Bank of Spain's report was upbeat for coming months. The economy should end this year and begin next "with higher levels of real growth that can be maintained medium-term."
"We are seeing an acceleration in private consumption that could lead us to GDP of 2.5 percent or higher in 1997," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
The government is predicting three percent growth next year, while Rojo on Thursday said it would be around 2.7 percent.
"Overall, we are expecting improvement," said Antonio Villarroya, analyst at Merrill Lynch in Madrid. "We expect private consumption to pick up substantially."
